I picked this game up for free off of Humble Bundle, and thought that it would be "just another free game" to add to my library. Boy, was I wrong...

Hacknet is an amazing game. What starts off as a seemingly simple game about hacking unfolds into a fully-fledged storyline, in which you eventually end up, for the greater good, [spoiler]taking down a new operating system, called Hacknet, that would have destroyed people's freedom.[/spoiler] The final line in the game's end sequence is particularly powerful: [spoiler]If all's gone right, there's just one copy of Hacknet left to delete - and you're looking at it.[/spoiler]

To put it as simply as possible: Get this game. It's amazing.
Seriously. Buy it now.

It has been a while since Humble offered a free game that I found worth picking up.

There's a pretty great offering of the no handholding progression/exploration in this game, even though the game doesn't punish you for not deleting your logs or if you fail to repel a hack on your system, it doesn't give a big flashing sign where to go for if you are stuck in some spot either a refreshing take from the modern games that have you chasing a quest marker all the time.
Sure the earlier missions do give a lot of hints and even provide you with server nodes so you don't have to connect to an IP manually. But after a while you're on your own.
Its not what you'd define as being casual game, but it is far from hardcore as if you get hacked you don't even get sent back to your last save even though there is a manual save system that also autosaves if you do certain story missions.
Plus the difficulty not high enough for my taste and I have no past experience with coding, just I played a bunch of harder puzzle games, it peaks with some optional side mission mid-game where you have to use commands to make a convincing document forgery using a template and legit documents as reference before inserting it into a database. And you don't see anything as complex and challenging from that point onward. Though kudos to the devs having a special note that that specific mission will not be easy, a nice touch for a not so casual element in a casual game.

About the advertised rabbithole, yes you'll have quite the localized rabbithole by the end of the game, the ending parts are amazing. But the general non main quest network web loses its shine very fast, and reavealing itself to be a three dimensional cardboard cutout. When you get to the midgame you see bulletin boards with lots of hacking jobs, dump servers with various files you can start working from on your own, highly secure mail systems with a lot of accounts, you can't crack, but can find passwords in other ways, random side stuff and easter eggs, plus the main quest.
But once you realize that most of the heaps of files you picked up from the filedumps are actually just material for bulletin quests that spawned prematurely before picking the contract, it starts to fall apart then once you get admin account for mail and scan through all accounts, you realize that most are empty just to fill up space.
And the lowest point happens when you do try to do the secret path on your second playthrough, which is very fun while it lasts, but you get promised more later before you get booted back to main mid-game and then the promised "more secret path" doesn't deliver. it seems to be as if it was cut in development, maybe the more refers to DLC but who knows...

Overall the game is fun, but lacking substantial side content, but you can still probably get 14 well spent hours 100%ing it.

Hacknet is to information security as Guitar Hero is to being a musician.  If you want to play music, Guitar Hero isn't really going to get you there.  But if you want to have fun and live your rock-n-roll fantasy, Guitar Hero is totally going to deliver.  Likewise, if you want to learn infosec... you're better off setting up a VM lab, firing up some vulnerable server images, and reading up how security tools work.  But if you want to live out a hax0r fantasy, Hacknet delivers a feel for hax0ring the Gibson without all that fuss.

The game itself is a sequence of increasingly complex puzzles set within a hackery theme.  A tutorial introduces you to the GUI and command-line interfaces you'll need employ in your new career as a wiley cyber ninja.  An unintrusive, moody synth soundtrack sets the tone.  Then you're a portscan away from seeing how deep the rabbit hole goes.

Recommended for those who are tech enthusiasts, find solving a puzzle fires a rush as much as a bass rumble and flash of pixels, and anyone wanting to live that hax0ring fantasy.

I got a free copy of [i]Hacknet[/i] from a promotion on Humble Bundle without really knowing what the game was and only started playing it because of the Spring Cleaning Event here on Steam. I only intended to play it for a little bit and then move on to something else.  ...I finished the game in one sitting. Which took most of the night when I was supposed to be sleeping and I barely even noticed. Never before would I have said that a game based almost entirely around typing computer run commands would hold my interest, but [i]man[/i] was I completely enthralled start to finish.

Not only did I finish the game in one sitting, but I also immediately started over to complete side quests and find bonus material I had missed the first time around. I still haven't finished the last achievement and found all the cool hidden bonus stuff.

[u]Plot[/u]
You have been introduced into the world of hacking by Bit, another hacker who has sent you a series of automated messages fearing his own demise. [spoiler]Yes, he is actually dead. I was about an inch away from crying when it was finally confirmed late in the game.[/spoiler] Through the course of the game you work with a number of hacker communities working both as a freelance digital vigilante and trying to unravel what really happened to Bit. The plot was exciting and I ended up emotionally invested. [spoiler]There is only one ending to the game, but there are optional side quests that alter way in which you get there, as well as bonus content that appears to only be available after a restart.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Most of the gameplay is done by typing various commands into your "terminal" in much the same fashion as old-school computer programs. If you've worked with DOS or similar systems you will probably have a bit of a leg up with the basic mechanics of the game. Using those commands you hack through the security systems of other computers, copying and deleting files off their harddrives and skipping from their computers to others in their network. These hacking attempts are sometimes straightforward, sometimes more complicated with critical thinking and puzzle cracking abilities required. The further you progress in the game the more difficult they become with most of the later hacking attempts becoming a fast-paced, speeding heart race against time. There is one(?) hidden mini-game that differs from this format. [spoiler]You can find it by taking the "Pointclicker" contract from Entropy[/spoiler] Overall, I didn't think the game was very difficult, although there were plenty of challenges to overcome. I did require a walkthrough the get myself out of a tricky spot, but that was mostly due to impatience. Probably the most difficult thing in the whole game was typing commands fast enough, so those who aren't good typists might struggle more with this game.

[u]Graphics & Music[/u]
[i]Hacknet[/i] has a very simple GUI for the entire game, fairly old-school computer but with a futuristic vibe. If the color scheme bothers you, just pay attention to the achievements. ;) [spoiler]My favorite was the L-e version, I do believe.[/spoiler] The music was all low-key techno music which I quite enjoyed. Sometimes it got a bit repetitive, but it changed according to where you were in the questline, so as long as you didn't get stuck in one place for a long time (like I did, before giving up and finding a walkthrough) it was fine.

[u]Bugs & Performance[/u]
Performance wise, the game ran perfectly well on my potato laptop with only 3GB of RAM. Since the game is done almost exclusively with the keyboard, having a real one is a must IMHO, but a mouse isn't necessary. I did just fine with a trackpad. The only "bug" I encountered when playing the game is that the game crashed whenever you tabbed out of it in fullscreen mode, even if you were chilling on the main menu. So make sure you save the game before attempting to open a different window!
The game has a well-developed story with an interesting game mechanic that I've been very into since I started.

[i]Hacknet[/i] is perhaps the first actual hacking game I've played outside of [i]Terminal Hacker[/i] (which was basically a guessing game similar to hangman).  It utilizes actual UNIX formatting in a mixture between a command prompt and a GUI layout.  In a way, it reminds me of my final heartbreaking days as an Information Technology major.

The story follows you, an unknown and obscure user who nobody would suspect of anything...until you get a message from a mysterious, yet well-known hacker who passed away.  Of all the people he chose as his spiritual successor, he chose you...someone who most likely has no connection to him whatsoever.  It's your job to avenge the fallen hacker's death and to honor his last wishes...while helping others or causing trouble along the way.

The hacking procedures are quite interesting and easy to learn, but become annoying after a while given that it's the same protocols every time with some new tricks thrown in every now and then.  Without a guide, [i]Hacknet[/i] really requires you to think and to look back at old references in your e-mails.   Soon enough, you'll encounter new obstacles, like increased security and even tracing, which adds a time limit and pressure to battle against.

Though I enjoyed [i]Hacknet[/i], I don't see too much replayability in it.  I was also not pleased with the repetitive nature of the game and there were cryptic moments where I needed to refer to a guide to proceed.  Cryptic and repetitive moments will quickly find themselves at your doorstep, but that's the name of the game, I suppose.

So...worth the price?  I suppose, but the repetitive bits make this [i]Hacknet[/i] rather unappealing.  It starts out simple, but you just end up doing the same thing for about 80% of the game...though the stressful tracing does make it a little more fun as some hacking tools require more time than others...so you have to balance your RAM as you try to hack through security.  Various bits aren't properly explained, too.  You sometimes need a new hacking method, but it's just not properly explained in my opinion.  It's moments like that that made me drop my IT major in college.  But to the point?  It's worth the price, but if you're a bargain hunter, $5 may be ideal.  Overall, I loved the idea and the execution was pretty good...but I wished that it was balanced a little more with even more to offer.

8/10  To be an expert hacker, you'll need a combination of the right software and wits...only one of them is provided by this game, the other must come from you.

This is technically probably the only straight hacking game I've played. Note, it's a "game", not real. There are certainly elements to this which are real. The behavior of cracking ports, passwords and being a script kiddie are some of them. Although the game is based on UNIX commands, the language used is a bit different. It is sort of a good introduction and learning tool (and the game does warn you about the implications), one has to remember that while the game isn't real, the action certainly is.

This game isn't perfect. There are certainly some "bugs" and game breaking behavior which will propel you away from 100% completion. And there are some things you can't do. Sometimes the difficulty is pretty hard, and other times, too easy. But you'll learn the commands well. In fact, this is mainly a typing simulator. For me, the controls were sticky, but it does work. What was far from attractive to me though was that accessing computer systems and servers were visually jumbled in the graphic execution, that it was difficult to see where lines meet. It was a little disorganized than it should be, and unfortunately this remains static.

But overall, the game is playable to an extent, and it focuses on a certain storyline. It may be possible for branching storylines, but for now Extensions (read: Workshop assets) offer other storyline amendments. As someone who is experienced coding with websites, for example, I feel right at home with the terminal interface a bit. Mainly, if you're the kind of person who wants to experience a bit of the thrill of hacking (without the actual consequences of course), have at it. There are certainly some easter eggs and extra content not used for the main game, but you can choose to have them to an extent for fun.

The aesthetic. The soundtrack. How friggen POWERFUL this game makes you feel. If you ever a fan of The Matrix, Hackers, or even Swordfish growing up, if you've ever wanted a hacker fantasy game that actually felt realistic while spamming out terminal commands, this is for you.

It's based on real UNIX commands and real IT conventions. It's a puzzle game at heart, with some text-input based puzzles with a bit of more modern GUI clicking here and there.

The game REALLY shines during the more intense sequences and it just cranks things up to 11.

The hidden IRC logs strewn about terminals you hack into, all from bash.org, is such a love letter to the early days of the Internet, late 90s mid 2000s hyper nerd circles.

I started getting into IT and wanted something like what I do but more exciting, more dangerous, more tense, and this satisfied my urge. The fact that there are extensions created for free by the community to give more replay just makes the deal sweeter.

Did I mention the soundtrack is incredible? I forget.

The story is top notch. Don't research anything about it, just play it. I haven't been affected by a story this intensely since playing Undertale, no exaggerating. (Less crying tho)

Tinker about the game files and folders, but only after finishing the game. Play it several times. Do things different. Think outside the box. Fight. Win.

Fun hacking game. It shows how hackers "really" work (flooding proxies and cracking firewalls, opening ports etc.), of course it's a bit modified to avoid teaching anyone actual hacking.

There is a reasonable freedom in approaching the various missions, as you progress through the ranks of hacker groups, until you reach a point where the story takes over and the main plot rides to its conclusion.

Fair warning, the game isn't exactly immune to bugs, I've had a quest not complete that blocked my progress that I had to work around by hacking into the gamesave file, a bit ironic, and achievements seem to be a bit tempermental.

Outside of that though, especially for the price, I would definately recommend it. The premise of a Metasploit OS on steroids certainly makes for an interesting concept and the developer did a great job on its execution. I greatly look forward to what they come out with next.
